title: Single Number
description: Brute force to optimized: counting every value versus a hash map versus XOR cancellation.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a non empty array of integers where every element appears exactly twice except for one element which appears only once, find that single element.

blocks.text: Given a non empty array of integers nums where every element appears exactly twice except for one element which appears only once, find that single element.

blocks.title: Analogy: The One Unpaired Sock in a Laundry Basket
blocks.text: Like sorting a basket of socks where every sock has a matching partner except for exactly one lone sock, and the goal is to identify that one unpaired sock without pairing up every sock by hand.

blocks.caption: Every value appears twice except one, which needs to be found

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["2 appears twice, 1 appears once","1 is the lone value","only one value in the array has a count different from 2"],["Answer","1","the value whose count is exactly 1"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 and 2 each appear twice, 4 appears once","4 is the lone value","checking every value's count shows only 4 occurs a single time"],["Answer","4","the value whose count is exactly 1"]]}

blocks.text: With a single element and nothing to pair it with, that element is trivially the answer, 1.
It helps to ask whether the guaranteed "everything paired except one" structure of this problem hints at a trick beyond simply counting.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force rescans the entire array once for every single element just to find that element's own count, redoing the same comparisons over and over.

Observation 2: A hash map fixes the repeated rescanning by tallying every value's count in a single pass, but it still needs O(n) extra space to store those counts.

Observation 3: The problem guarantees every value appears exactly twice except one, and XOR has two properties tailor made for this: a value XORed with itself is 0, and a value XORed with 0 leaves it unchanged; XORing every element together, in any order, cancels every paired value down to 0 and leaves only the lone value behind.

Observation 4: Tracing nums = [4,1,2,1,2] confirms it, XORing 4, 1, 2, 1, 2 together in order cancels the two 1s and the two 2s completely, leaving exactly 4, the answer, using nothing but a single running integer.
Recognizing that "paired except one" is precisely the structure XOR cancellation was made for is what turns a counting problem into a single pass, constant space one.
For every value, count how many times it appears by scanning the whole array, and return the value whose count is exactly 1.

items: For every index i, count how many times nums[i] appears across the entire array.
If that count is 1, return nums[i].

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every element is treated as its own query, rescanning the full array to count its occurrences, since there is no memory of counts already computed.
The moment a count of exactly 1 is found, the function returns immediately rather than finishing every remaining index.

blocks.text: Every value's true count is directly computed, so the one value appearing only once is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), rescanning the whole array for every element.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.
Limitation: the same counts get recomputed repeatedly whenever a paired value is revisited, instead of being counted just once per distinct value.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it rescans the entire array once per element, recomputing the same counts repeatedly for every paired value.

What a hash map fixes: tallying every value's count in a single pass eliminates all the repeated rescanning, at the cost of O(n) extra space.

What the "paired except one" guarantee enables beyond that: since every value except one appears an even number of times (exactly twice), XOR, which cancels a value with itself back to 0, can eliminate every pair without ever storing a single count.

The core idea: XOR every element together in one pass; every paired value cancels out completely, leaving only the lone value, with no extra data structure at all.

Count every value exactly once using a hash map from value to frequency, built in a single pass. Once every count is known, the value whose count equals 1 is the answer. Then notice that XOR offers an even better path: any value XORed with itself is 0, and any value XORed with 0 is unchanged, so XORing every element of the array together causes every paired value to cancel out completely, leaving only the single unpaired value behind.
Build a frequency map in one pass, then scan it for the value with a count of 1.

blocks.caption: Optimized: count every value once, then find the one with a count of 1

blocks.text: Every value's true final count is captured in the map after a single pass, so scanning the map for the one entry whose count is 1 is guaranteed to find the correct lone value.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A value's final tallied count is 2","It is skipped while scanning the map","Correctly excluded since it is a paired value"],["A value's final tallied count is 1","It is returned as soon as found","Correctly identified as the lone unpaired value"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to count, one pass over the distinct values.
Space: O(n), for the frequency map in the worst case.

items: A single pass builds the frequency map, incrementing each value's tally as it is seen.
A second pass over the map, not the original array, is enough to locate the one entry whose count is exactly 1.

blocks.text: XOR has two properties that make this problem elegant: any value XORed with itself is 0, and any value XORed with 0 is unchanged. XORing every element of the array together, in any order, causes every paired value to cancel out completely (since it appears exactly twice), leaving only the single unpaired value behind, with no extra data structure at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Running XOR"],"rows":[["Start at 0","0"],["XOR with 4","4"],["XOR with 1","4 XOR 1"],["XOR with 2","4 XOR 1 XOR 2"],["XOR with 1 again (cancels the earlier 1)","4 XOR 2"],["XOR with 2 again (cancels the earlier 2)","4"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: XOR every value together, every pair cancels, the lone value remains

items: The running result starts at 0, XOR's identity value, so the very first element passes through unchanged.
Every element is XORed into the running result exactly once, in whatever order they appear, since XOR is commutative and associative and never depends on ordering.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per element.
Space: O(1), only one running value is kept.

blocks.text: This problem is the standard introduction to XOR cancellation, a pattern that reappears throughout bit manipulation problems whenever values are guaranteed to occur in pairs except for one exception.

items: Assuming XOR cancellation requires the paired values to be adjacent or in any particular order, when XOR is fully commutative and associative, so the order of processing never matters.
Reaching for a hash map by default without considering that the guaranteed "everything paired except one" structure is exactly what makes the XOR trick possible.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single element array","Trivially its own answer, since XORing one value with the initial 0 leaves it unchanged."],["Negative numbers","XOR handles them identically to positive numbers through their two's complement bit representation."]]}

blocks.text: Mention explicitly which two properties of XOR make this trick work (self cancellation and identity with 0), since stating this reasoning is what distinguishes genuine understanding from a memorized trick.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: XOR cancellation instead of a hash map.
If the interviewer says "does the order of processing matter", think: no, XOR is commutative and associative.
If the interviewer says "what if values could appear three times instead of two", think: plain XOR cancellation no longer works, a different bit counting technique is needed instead.

items: What would you do if every value appeared three times instead of two, except for one lone value?
What if there were exactly two lone values instead of one, each appearing only once?
Why does the order in which elements are XORed together never affect the final result?
How does XOR treat negative numbers compared to positive numbers?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Further optimized (XOR cancellation): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: XOR cancellation, exploiting a guaranteed "paired except one" structure.
Core Idea: XORing every element together cancels every paired value to 0, leaving only the single unpaired value behind.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both the hash map and XOR approaches.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the hash map, O(1) for XOR cancellation.
Most Important Observation: a guaranteed pairing structure in the input is often a direct signal to reach for XOR instead of counting.
Interview Difficulty: the brute force and hash map versions are easy to reach; producing the XOR insight unprompted is what separates a strong answer.
One line memory trick: XOR everything together, pairs vanish, the lone value survives.
